passages.t: Back to Bethel, and the foreign gods buried
passages.happening:
God speaks to Jacob: “Arise, go up to Bethel, and settle there. Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau” (verse 1).

Jacob tells his household, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you. Purify yourselves and change your garments” (verse 2). “I will build an altar there to God, who answered me in my day of distress. He has been with me wherever I have gone” (verse 3).

They give him their foreign gods and their earrings, “and Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem” (verse 4). As they travel, “a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob's sons” (verse 5).

At Bethel Jacob builds an altar and names the place El-bethel, ‘the God of Bethel’ (verses 6-7). There Deborah, Rebekah's old nurse, dies and is buried under an oak. Jacob names it Allon-bachuth, ‘oak of weeping’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
After the horror of chapter 34, God speaks. It is the first time he has spoken since Jacob came home. He sends Jacob back to the place where it all began.

Twenty years earlier, running from Esau, Jacob slept at Bethel and dreamed of the stairway. He made a vow there: if God brought him home safely, the LORD would be his God and the stone would be God's house (28:20-22). Jacob has been home for some time and has not gone back. Now God reminds him.

Jacob's household has been carrying other gods. Rachel stole her father's household gods (31:19), and there may have been others among the servants and the captives from Shechem. Before they go to meet God, they hand them over. They wash and put on clean clothes, an outward sign of a new start. The earrings may have been charms tied to other gods.

Jacob buries them all under a great tree. He does not keep them in a box in case. He leaves them in the ground and walks away.

Jacob was afraid the towns around would destroy his family (34:30). God answers that fear. A terror falls on the towns, and no one follows. God protects the family in spite of what the sons did, not because of it.

Then a small, tender verse. Deborah, the nurse who came with Rebekah from Haran long ago (24:59), dies. She was a servant. Genesis gives her a name, a grave, and a tree named for the tears shed over her.
passages.later:
Centuries later, at the same town of Shechem, Joshua called Israel to make the same choice: “get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel” (Joshua 24:23). Samuel called for it again (1 Samuel 7:3).

Before God met Israel at Mount Sinai, the people washed their clothes (Exodus 19:10). John writes, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).
passages.asks: Jacob's family buried their idols before they went to meet God. Ask what you are carrying that competes with God for your trust. Then ask whether you are ready to bury it, and not keep it close in case.

passages.happening:
“God appeared to him again and blessed him” (verse 9).

“Though your name is Jacob, you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be Israel” (verse 10).

God says, “I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply” (verse 11). Nations and kings will come from him. “The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give this land to your descendants after you” (verse 12).

God goes up from him (verse 13). Jacob sets up a stone pillar, pours out a drink offering on it, anoints it with oil, and calls the place Bethel (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
This is the second time Jacob is given the name Israel. The first time was in the dark at the river Jabbok, after a night of wrestling (32:28). Now God says it again, in daylight, at Bethel, with no struggle at all. The new name is not a prize Jacob won. It is a gift God confirms.

God gathers up the promises of the whole book. ‘Be fruitful and multiply’ are the words of the first blessing on human beings (1:28). ‘Kings shall descend from you’ was promised to Abraham (17:6). The land was promised to Abraham and Isaac. All of it now rests on Jacob.

‘God Almighty’ translates El Shaddai, the name God used to Abraham (17:1). Its exact meaning is debated, but ‘Almighty’ has been the usual rendering since ancient translations.

A drink offering is wine or another liquid poured out before God as a gift. This is the first time the Bible mentions one. Jacob does at Bethel exactly what he did twenty years before: he sets up a stone, pours oil on it, and names the place ‘house of God’ (28:18-19). The circle is closed. The vow is kept.
passages.later:
Israel's later law gave drink offerings a place in daily worship (Numbers 28:7). Paul uses the picture for his own life poured out for others: “even if I am being poured out like a drink offering” (Philippians 2:17).

The promise of kings came true in Saul and then in David, and Matthew opens his Gospel with “Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1).
passages.asks: God gave Jacob his new name again, without a struggle. Ask whether you still think God's love for you is something you have to wrestle out of him. Then ask what it would mean to receive what he has already said.

passages.happening:
They set out from Bethel. On the road, still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel goes into labor, “and her labor was difficult” (verse 16).

The midwife tells her, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son” (verse 17).

Rachel is dying. With her last breath “she named him Ben-oni. But his father called him Benjamin” (verse 18).

“So Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)” (verse 19). Jacob sets up a pillar on her grave, and the narrator says it marks Rachel's tomb “to this day” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
This is the saddest scene in Jacob's life. Rachel is the wife he loved, the one he served fourteen years for. Years ago she cried, ‘Give me children, or I will die’ (30:1). When her first son Joseph was born, she named him with a prayer for another son (30:24). Now the other son comes, and it costs her life.

The midwife's words are kind: ‘Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.’ Her prayer has been answered. But she does not live to raise him.

With her last breath Rachel names the baby Ben-oni. It most likely means ‘son of my sorrow’, though the word can also mean ‘son of my strength’. Jacob renames him Benjamin, ‘son of the right hand’. In the Bible the right hand stands for strength and favor. Jacob will not let his youngest son carry a name of grief all his life.

Rachel is buried by the road, not in the family grave at Machpelah where Abraham and Sarah lie. Jacob marks the place with a stone. Years later, dying in Egypt, he will still speak of it: “to my sorrow Rachel died along the way” (48:7).

Where exactly was the grave? Verse 19 places it on the way to Ephrath, and a note says that is Bethlehem. A traditional tomb at Bethlehem's edge has been honored for many centuries. But 1 Samuel 10:2 puts Rachel's tomb ‘in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin’, north of Jerusalem. Some scholars think the Bethlehem note reflects a later identification; others hold that the tomb lay near Bethlehem all along. The question is open.
passages.later:
Rachel's grief became a picture for the whole people. When Judah's sons were carried into exile, Jeremiah heard her: “A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (Jeremiah 31:15). God answers her in the next verse: “your children will return from the land of the enemy” (Jeremiah 31:16).

Matthew quotes Jeremiah's words when King Herod kills the little boys of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18). The mother who died on the road to Bethlehem weeps again for Bethlehem's children.
passages.hard:
A word of care. Some readers come to this passage having lost a wife, a mother, a daughter or a baby in childbirth. Rachel's story does not explain that kind of loss, and it does not make it small. The Bible records it, and Jacob carried it to the end of his life. Your grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a grief counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

And a word for anyone who grew up without a mother because of a birth like this one. Benjamin did too. Your father may have given you a new name, as Jacob did. But it is right to grieve the mother you never knew.
passages.asks: Rachel named her son for her sorrow, and Jacob named him for hope. Ask whether there is a loss in your life you have never let yourself grieve. Then ask how God might give a new name to what still hurts, without asking you to pretend it did not happen.

passages.t: Reuben and Bilhah; the twelve sons
passages.happening:
“Israel again set out and pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder” (verse 21).

“While Israel was living in that region, Reuben went in and slept with his father's concubine Bilhah, and Israel heard about it” (verse 22).

Then the twelve sons of Jacob are listed by their mothers. Leah's sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun. Rachel's sons: Joseph and Benjamin. Bilhah's sons: Dan and Naphtali. Zilpah's sons: Gad and Asher (verses 22-26).
passages.hearers:
Reuben is Jacob's firstborn, Leah's eldest son. Bilhah is Rachel's servant, the mother of two of his brothers. A concubine was a secondary wife with fewer rights than a full wife.

One verse tells it, and then the story moves on. Israel hears about it, and the text says nothing more. There is no confrontation and no punishment, not yet.

Bilhah is an enslaved woman. Once again she has no say. Genesis does not give her one word. We do not know what she wanted or what this did to her. Her silence in the story is part of what it shows, as it was when she was first given to Jacob (30:3-4).

Why would Reuben do this? In the ancient world, taking a ruler's concubine could be a claim to take his place. Absalom did this to his father David's concubines to show that he had seized the throne (2 Samuel 16:21-22). Many readers think Reuben, the firstborn, was grabbing at his father's authority too soon. Rachel had just died, and Bilhah was her servant.

Some rabbinic teachers, uneasy with the plain words, read the verse differently. The Talmud, a great collection of Jewish teaching, records a view that Reuben only disturbed his father's bed, moving it out of Bilhah's tent to defend his mother Leah's honor. Most readers take the words as they stand.

Then comes the list of twelve. Reuben is still called ‘the firstborn’. The list closes Jacob's family story. These twelve sons will become the twelve tribes of Israel.
passages.later:
Jacob gives his verdict at the end of his life: “you will no longer excel, because you went up to your father's bed, onto my couch, and defiled it” (Genesis 49:4). Chronicles says Reuben's birthright was given to the sons of Joseph “because Reuben defiled his father's bed” (1 Chronicles 5:1).

In the last book of the Bible, the names of the twelve tribes are written on the gates of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12).
passages.asks: Reuben grabbed at what was not yet his, and Bilhah paid without a voice. Ask where you are tempted to seize something before its time, and who else would pay for it. Then ask whose silence you have not noticed.

passages.t: Isaac dies, and both sons bury him
passages.happening:
“Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had stayed” (verse 27).

“And Isaac lived 180 years” (verse 28).

“Then he breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of years. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Jacob comes home to the father he deceived. Genesis tells us nothing of what they said to each other. The son who left in fear has come back.

Hebron lies in the hills south of Jerusalem. Mamre, near it, is where Abraham pitched his tent, and where he bought the cave of Machpelah as the family grave (chapter 23).

‘Gathered to his people’ is the Bible's way of saying a man has joined those who died before him. ‘Old and full of years’ means a long and complete life.

The last line is quiet and moving. Esau and Jacob, the twins who fought before they were born, stand together at their father's grave. Isaac and Ishmael did the same for Abraham (25:9). The rivalry ends in a shared duty.

One small puzzle. If you add up the ages Genesis gives elsewhere, Isaac was still alive when Joseph was sold in chapter 37, and lived about twelve more years. The book tells his death here to finish one generation's story before the next begins. Genesis often finishes one person's story before it turns to the next.
passages.later:
Isaac's two sons buried him together, as Isaac and Ishmael had buried Abraham: “His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah” (Genesis 25:9).

Jesus said God calls himself “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, and added, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).
passages.asks: Two brothers who had been enemies stood at one grave. Ask whether there is someone you are estranged from whom you will one day stand beside, at a grave or before God. Then ask whether peace has to wait that long.
